# Dynamic framework for edge-connectivity maintenance of simple graphs

Blażej Wróbel <sup>∗</sup>

March 10, 2026

**Abstract**

We present a framework for dynamically maintaining _k_-edge-connectivity of an undirected simple graph _G_ under edge insertions and deletions, where _k_ is a fixed constant. After an edge insertion, the algorithm identifies and removes a distinct redundant edge to maintain sparsity, in _O(k_log_n_) amortized time. After an edge deletion that reduces \(\lambda(G)\) below _k_, the algorithm restores _k_-edge-connectivity by adding at most two new edges (excluding the deleted edge), in _O(k_<sup>3/2</sup>_n_<sup>3/2</sup>) time. The insertion procedure combines Nagamochi–Ibaraki sparse certificates with Link-Cut Trees; the deletion procedure uses a single maximum-flow computation on the sparsified graph. Throughout all updates, the graph is maintained with _O(kn_) edges.

### 1 Introduction

Edge-connectivity is one of the fundamental measures of network reliability and fault tolerance. A graph is _k_-edge-connected if the removal of fewer than _k_ edges cannot disconnect it. We study the problem of actively maintaining _k_-edge-connectivity: given a graph _G_ with \(\lambda(G)\ge k\), the goal is to preserve this invariant under edge insertions and deletions by modifying the graph itself - not merely reporting whether the invariant holds. An edge insertion may make an existing edge redundant for _k_-edge-connectivity, while an edge deletion may reduce \(\lambda(G)\) below _k_. We address both cases:

1. Redundancy Elimination (Post-Addition): after insertion of a new edge _e<sub>new</sub>_={_u,v_}, local edge-connectivity between its endpoints may be greater than _k_. To maintain structural sparsity - specifically ensuring |_E_|=_O(kn_) - we identify and remove an existing edge \(e_{old}=\{x,y\}(e_{old}\neq e_{new})\) for which the condition \(\lambda(x,y;(G\cup\{e_{new}\})\backslash\{e_{old}\})\ge k\) (see Section 3 for definition of \(\lambda(x,y;G)\)) is met. This ensures that the graph remains sparse and _k_-edge-connected.

2. Connectivity Restoration (Post-Removal): after removal of an existing edge _e<sub>del</sub>_, the global edge-connectivity may drop below the required threshold, i.e., \(\lambda(G\backslash\{e_{del}\})<k\). In such cases, the framework computes and inserts a minimal set of augmenting edges \(E_{aug}(e_{del}\notin E_{aug})\) such that the condition \(\lambda((G\backslash\{e_{del}\})\cup E_{aug})\ge k\) holds.

Beyond its theoretical interest, our framework is motivated by settings where a network’s link structure must be actively maintained under dynamic changes. A natural application of Connectivity Restoration arises in survivable telecommunications network design, where nodes represent routers and edges represent physical communication links. Such networks are designed to be sparse and _k_-edge-connected so that data transmission survives up to _k_-1 simultaneous link failures [8]. When a link is lost - due to hardware malfunction or fiber cut - the operator must provision new links to restore the required redundancy. Our framework models this directly: the failed link is an edge deletion, and the algorithm computes the minimal set of new links to restore invariant \(\lambda(G)\ge k\).

<sup>∗</sup>Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Poland

In wireless sensor networks, topology control protocols seek sparse communication topologies that preserve connectivity, since maintaining fewer active links reduces both energy consumption and radio interference \[13\]. Our Redundancy Elimination task provides an algorithmic primitive aligned with this objective: when a new link becomes available, the framework detects and removes an existing link that is no longer necessary for _k_-edge- connectivity, keeping the network sparse with _O(kn_) edges.

## 2 Related work

Computing the minimum cut in an undirected graph is a classic problem with a long history. Early approaches relied on network flow techniques; the Gomory-Hu \[6\] tree construction reduces the problem to _n_-1 maximum flow computations. Karger \[10\] introduced a randomized algorithm based on tree packings that finds the global minimum cut in _O(m_log<sup>3</sup>_n_) time with high probability. In the deterministic setting, Henzinger, Rao, and Wang \[9\] gave an algorithm for determining graph’s edge-connectivity, running in _O(m_log<sup>2</sup>(_n_)log(log<sup>2</sup>(_n_))) time. Li \[11\] presented a deterministic algorithm for finding minimum-cuts in weighted undirected graphs running in _m_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time.

The problem of maintaining the minimum cut in a dynamically changing graph has been studied extensively, with a primary focus on efficiently reporting the value of the minimum cut rather than actively enforcing a connectivity invariant. Thorup \[16\] gave a deterministic fully dynamic algorithm that maintains the value of the minimum cut in \(\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})\) (see Section 3) worst-case time per update. For the incremental setting, Goranci et al. \[7\] achieved _O_(log<sup>3</sup>(_n_)log(log<sup>2</sup>(_n_))) amortized update time by maintaining a set of edge-disjoint spanning forests - a sparse certificate that preserves connectivity properties. Our approach to redundancy elimination (Section 4) builds on a similar structural insight: by actively maintaining a certificate of size _O(kn_), we can efficiently identify and remove redundant edges in _O(k_log_n_) amortized time per edge addition. For connectivity restoration (Section 5), we exploit the specific properties of Dinic’s algorithm \[4\] on unit-capacity networks. While the general weighted case requires _O(n_<sup>2</sup>_m_) time, Even and Tarjan \[5\] showed that the complexity improves to _O_(min(_n_<sup>2/3</sup>_,m_<sup>1/2</sup>)_m_) for unit capacities. This bound is critical to our edge-connectivity restoration strategy.

## 3 Preliminaries and notation

We consider unweighted, simple, undirected graphs _G_=(_V,E_) with a vertex set _V_ and edge set _E_, where |_V_|=_n_ and |_E_|=_m_, using these parameters primarily to describe the computational complexity of the proposed algorithms. To simplify the asymptotic analysis, we employ the notation \(\tilde{O}(f(n))\) to denote _O(f(n_)log_<sup>k</sup>n_) for some constant \(k\ge 0\), thereby suppressing polylogarithmic factors; crucially, this notation never obscures polynomial factors. When considering several graphs, we denote the respective sets of a graph _G_ as _V(G_) and _E(G_) to avoid ambiguity. Furthermore, we denote an undirected edge connecting vertices _u_ and _v_ as the set {_u,v_}, while a directed edge (arc) from _u_ to _v_ is denoted by the ordered pair (_u,v_). For an edge _e_={_u,v_}, we write endpoints(_e_) to denote the pair of vertices incident to _e_. In pseudocode, the assignment \((u,v)\leftarrow\) endpoints(_e_) binds the two endpoints of _e_ to the variables _u_ and _v_ in arbitrary order.

For any two vertices \(u,v\in V\) , let \(\lambda(u,v;G)\) denote the local edge-connectivity, defined as the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths between _u_ and _v_ in _G_. The global edge- connectivity of _G_, denoted by \(\lambda(G)\), is the minimum local edge-connectivity over all pairs of vertices, i.e. \(\lambda(G)=min_{u,v\in V}\lambda(u,v;G)\).

The parameter _k_ represents the required global edge-connectivity and is treated as a fixed integer constant throughout the paper.

For any subset of vertices \(S\subseteq V\) and \(S\neq\emptyset\), let _G_\[_S_\]=(_S,E_\[_S_\]) denote the subgraph induced by _S_, where \(E[S]=\{\{u,v\}\in E|u,v\in S\}\) represents the set of edges with endpoints entirely contained within _S_. A cut is a partition of the vertex set into two disjoint sets \((S,\bar{S})\) such that \(S\cup\bar{S}=V\) and \(S\cap\bar{S}=\emptyset\). The cardinality of the cut is the number of edges with one endpoint in _S_ and the other in \(\bar{S}\). Namely,

\(|(S,\bar{S})|=|E\backslash(E[S]\cup E[\bar{S}])|.\)

Throughout this paper, we use the terms cut size and cut cardinality interchangeably. By Menger’s theorem \[3\], the local edge-connectivity \(\lambda(u,v;G)\) is equivalent to the size of the minimum cut separating _u_ and _v_.

We use \(G\cup\{e\}\) and _G_\\{_e_} to represent the graph resulting from the insertion or deletion of edge _e_, respectively. In the context of our edge-connectivity maintenance algorithms, _e<sub>new</sub>_ refers to a newly inserted edge, while _e<sub>old</sub>_ refers to an existing edge identified for removal during Redundancy Elimination. Similarly, _e<sub>del</sub>_ denotes an edge targeted for deletion by Connectivity Restoration, and _E<sub>aug</sub>_ represents the set of augmenting edges computed by the framework to restore edge-connectivity.

To address problems defined in Section 1 efficiently, we rely on a fundamental graph- theoretic property regarding the locality of connectivity changes. The following lemma characterizes the structural impact of removing an edge from a _k_-edge-connected graph,

**Lemma 1.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be an undirected and k-edge-connected graph and e_={_u,v_} _be an edge in E. Let_ \(G'=G\backslash\{e\}\)_. If_ \(\lambda(G')<k\)_, then_ \(\lambda(u,v;G)=k-1\)_. Furthermore, any cut in_ \(G'\) _which cardinality is less than k must separate u and v._

_Proof._ Consider any cut \((S,\bar{S})\) in \(G'\) with cardinality strictly less than _k_. Since the original graph _G_ is _k_-edge-connected, the cardinality of this cut in _G_ must have been at least _k_. The removal of the single edge _e_={_u,v_} can reduce size of a cut by at most one, and this occurs if and only if _e_ crosses the cut (i.e., \(u\in S\) and \(v\in\bar{S}\) or vice versa). Therefore, for the cut’s capacity to drop below _k_ in \(G'\), its original capacity must have been exactly _k_, and it must separate _u_ and _v_, resulting in a final cardinality of exactly _k_-1.

We use this lemma directly in the restoration algorithm of Section 5.

## 4 Restoration after Edge Addition

### 4.1 Sparse certificate maintenance

To identify and eliminate redundant edges, we use a sparse certificate as introduced by Nagamochi and Ibaraki \[12\]. The edge set of a graph _G_ can be decomposed into a sequence of edge-disjoint spanning forests _F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>_,...,F<sub>m</sub>_. For maintaining _k_-edge-connectivity, it suffices to maintain only the first _k_ forests, which form the sparse certificate \(G_{cert}=\bigcup_{i=1}^kF_i\). The following lemma establishes that this subgraph preserves the relevant edge-connectivity properties:

**Lemma 2** (From \[12\])**.** _For a simple graph G_=(_V,E), let F<sub>i</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>i</sub>_) _be a maximal spanning forest in_ \(G-E_1\cup E_2\cup\cdots\cup E_{i-1}\) _for i_=1,2_,...,|E|, where possibly_ \(E_i=E_{i+1}=\cdots=E_{|E|}=\emptyset\) _for some i. Then each spanning subgraph_ \(G_i=(V,E_1\cup E_2\cup\cdots\cup E_i)\) _satisfies_

\(\lambda(x,y;G_i)\ge min\{\lambda(x,y;G),i\}\text{\textit{for all}}x,y\in V,\) (1)

_where_ \(\lambda(x,y;H)\) _denotes the local edge-connectivity between x and y in graph H._

In particular, if \(k\le\lambda(G)\), the subgraph \(G_k=\left(V,\bigcup_{i=1}^kE_i\right)\) is itself _k_-edge-connected.

The sparse certificate is constructed using the linear-time sparsification method of Nagamochi and Ibaraki \[12\], presented in Algorithm 1. The procedure partitions _E_ into a sequence of edge-disjoint forests _E_<sub>1</sub>_,E_<sub>2</sub>_,...,E_<sub>|_E_|</sub> in a single pass over the graph. Each vertex _v_ maintains a rank _r(v_), initially set to zero, that tracks the number of forests containing an edge incident to _v_. At each step, the algorithm selects an unscanned vertex _x_ with maximum rank and assigns each unscanned edge _e_={_x,y_} to forest _E_<sub>_r(y_)+1</sub>. Since _y_ has no edge in _E_<sub>_r(y_)+1</sub> at the time of processing, this assignment preserves acyclicity. Ranks are then updated: _r(x_) (if _r(x_)=_r(y_)) and _r(y_) are incremented. Each edge is thus placed into the lowest-index forest that can accept it in _O_(1) time, yielding an overall running time of _O(m_). We use this procedure as a preprocessing step to construct the sparse certificate before handling dynamic edge additions.

**Algorithm 2** Function to modify forest represented by Link-Cut structure. function TryAdd(LC,u,v)
\(uRoot\leftarrow LC.\text{FindRoot}(u)\)
\(vRoot\leftarrow LC.\text{FindRoot}(v)\)
if \(uRoot\neq vRoot\) then
LC.evert(u)
LC.link(u, v)
return null
else
\(p\leftarrow LC.\text{parent}(u)\)
LC.cut(u)
LC.link(u, v)
return (u, p)
end if
end function **Algorithm 3** Handling edge addition in a sparse certificate. procedure HandleAddition(e)
\((u,v)\leftarrow endpoints(e)\triangleright 1\). Define endpoints of edge e
\(result\leftarrow TryAdd(LC_1,u,v)\)
if \(result\neq\text{null then}\)
\((x,y)\leftarrow endpoints(result)\)
\(i\leftarrow 2\)
while \(i\le k\) do
\(result\leftarrow TryAdd(LC_i,x,y)\)
if result=null then break
else
\((x,y)\leftarrow endpoints(result)\)
\(i\leftarrow i+1\)
end if
end while
end if
end procedure F1 F2 F3 V1 V2 V3 V1 V2 V3 V1 V2 V3 {v1, v4} V4 V5 V6 V4 V5 V6 V4 V5 V6 inserted edge displaced edge absorbed edge Figure 1: HandleAddition({_v_4_,v_6}): edge {_v_4_,v_6} displaces {_v_1_,v_4} from _F_1; edge {_v_1_,v_4} is absorbed into _F_2. _F_3 remains unchanged.

## 4.2 Correctness analysis

We first establish that TryAdd preserves the forest structure (Fact 1, Corollary 1), then that component connectivity is invariant under edge swaps (Lemma 3), and finally that HandleAddition preserves _k_-edge-connectivity (Lemma 4, Theorem 5).

**Fact 1.** _Let F_=(_V,E<sub>F</sub>_) _be a spanning forest and let_ \(e=\{u,v\}\notin E_F\).

1. _If u and v are in different connected components of F, then_ \((V,E_F\cup\{e\})\) _is a forest._<tbc>

_2._ _If u and v are in the same connected component and P<sub>uv</sub> is the path connecting them in F, then for any_ \(e'\in P_{uv}\)_, the graph_ \((V,(E_F\cup\{e\})\backslash\{e'\})\) _is a spanning forest._

**Corollary 1.** _Let F_=(_V,E<sub>F</sub>_) _be the forest represented by Link-Cut tree LC, and let e_={_u,v_} _be an edge not in E<sub>F</sub>. After executing_ TryAdd(_LC, u, v), the forest represented by LC remains a valid spanning forest._

**Lemma 3.** _Let F<sub>i</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>i</sub>_) _be a spanning forest and let_ \(F'_i\) _be the forest obtained by replacing an edge_ \(\{u,\text{parent}(u)\}\in E_i\) _with an edge_ \(\{u,v\}\notin E_i\)_, where u and v are in the same connected component of F<sub>i</sub>. For any pair of vertices_ \(x,y\in V\)_, x and y are connected in F<sub>i</sub> if and only if they are connected in_ \(F'_i\).

_Proof._ Let _C_ be the component of _F<sub>i</sub>_ containing _u_ and _v_. Removing {_u,_parent(_u_)} partitions _V(C_) into two subsets: _V<sub>u</sub>_, the vertices of the subtree rooted at _u_, and _V(C_)\\_V<sub>u</sub>_. Since \(v\in V(C)\backslash V_u\), adding {_u,v_} reconnects these two subsets into a single connected component. No edges incident to vertices outside _V(C_) are affected, so the remaining components of _F<sub>i</sub>_ are unchanged.

**Lemma 4.** _If vertices_ \(u,v\in V\) _are connected in forest F<sub>k</sub>, then they are connected in every preceding forest F<sub>j</sub> for_ \(1\le j<k\).

_Proof._ Fix _j_ with \(1\le j<k\). Since the forests _E_<sub>1</sub>_,...,E_<sub>|_E_|</sub> are pairwise edge-disjoint and _j\<k_, we have \(E_k\subseteq E\backslash\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{j-1}E_i\right)\). If _u_ and _v_ are connected in _F<sub>k</sub>_, there exists a path \(P_{uv}\subseteq E_k\), and by the inclusion above, \(P_{uv}\subseteq E\backslash\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{j-1}E_i\right)\). Since _F<sub>j</sub>_ is a maximal spanning forest of \(E\backslash\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{j-1}E_i\right)\) (Lemma 2.5 in \[12\]), _u_ and _v_ are connected in _F<sub>j</sub>_.

The following theorem is the central correctness result for HandleAddition algorithm; its proof combines Lemmas 3 and 4.

**Theorem 5.** _Let_ \(G'=\left(V,\bigcup_{i=1}^kE_i\right)\) _be the sparse certificate maintained by Algorithm 3. If_ HandleAddition_(e<sub>new</sub>) discards an edge e<sub>old</sub>_={_u,v_} _(e_\(_{new}\neq e_{old}\)_), then_ \(\lambda(u,v;(G'\cup\{e_{new}\})\backslash\{e_{old}\})\ge k\).

_Proof._ We maintain the following invariant: after every TryAdd operation, each forest _F<sub>j</sub>_ (\(1\le j\le k\)) is a maximal spanning forest of \(E\backslash(\bigcup_{i=1}^{j-1}E_i)\), and the forests _E_<sub>1</sub>_,...,E<sub>k</sub>_ remain pairwise edge-disjoint. The invariant holds initially by the Nagamochi-Ibaraki construction (Lemma 2). We first show it is preserved by HandleAddition, then use it to conclude _e<sub>old</sub>_ redundancy.

We will consider two cases. First, let us assume that TryAdd(_LC<sub>j</sub>_, _x_, _y_) returns null value (edge is absorbed into forest _F<sub>j</sub>_). The edge {_x,y_} connects two connected components of _F<sub>j</sub>_. Since two connected components of _F<sub>j</sub>_ are connected by {_x,y_}, any edge from \(\bigcup_{i=j+1}^kE_i\) still induce a cycle in _F<sub>j</sub>_, so _F<sub>j</sub>_ remains maximal. For each _l\>j_, the edges are moved between forests with edge sets _E_<sub>1</sub>_,E_<sub>2</sub>_,...,E<sub>j</sub>_ - contained in \(\bigcup_{i=1}^{l-1}E_i\) - and the new edge _e<sub>new</sub>_ is present in _E_ and _E_<sub>1</sub>. Thus, the set of available edges \(E\backslash\bigcup_{i=1}^{l-1}E_i\) remains unchanged, so _F<sub>l</sub>_ remains maximal for _l\>j_.

Now, assume that TryAdd(_LC<sub>j</sub>_, _x_, _y_) returns non-null value (edge was displaced). The operation replaces one edge in _E<sub>j</sub>_ with another, and by Lemma 3 the connected components of _F<sub>j</sub>_ are unchanged. Disjointness is maintained because the displaced edge is removed from _E<sub>j</sub>_ before being passed to the next forest. Before the operation, _F<sub>j</sub>_ is a maximal spanning forest of \(E\backslash\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{j-1}E_i\right)\), so every edge in \(\bigcup_{i=j+1}^kE_i\) induces a cycle in _F<sub>j</sub>_. Since TryAdd<tbc>

preserves connected components of _F<sub>j</sub>_ (Lemma 3), every such edge still creates a cycle. The displaced edge also has both endpoints in the same component of _F<sub>j</sub>_, so it would induce a cycle if re-added. Therefore _F<sub>j</sub>_ remains maximal.

Let _e<sub>old</sub>_={_u,w_} be the edge discarded from _F<sub>k</sub>_. Since _w_=parent(_u_), the vertices _u_ and _w_ were in the same connected component of _F<sub>k</sub>_ before the swap, and they remain so afterward by Lemma 3. By Lemma 4, _u_ and _w_ are connected in every _F<sub>j</sub>_ for \(1\le j\le k\). Each forest _F<sub>j</sub>_ therefore contains a path _P<sub>j</sub>_ from _u_ to _w_ using edges from _E<sub>j</sub>_. Since _E_<sub>1</sub>_,E_<sub>2</sub>_,...,E<sub>k</sub>_ are pairwise disjoint, the paths _P_<sub>1</sub>_,P_<sub>2</sub>_,...,P<sub>k</sub>_ are edge-disjoint. Hence \(\lambda(u,w;G')\ge k\).

### 4.3 Complexity analysis of sparse certificate maintenance algorithm

Initialization consists of two steps: computing the forest decomposition _F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>_,...,F<sub>k</sub>_ via Algorithm 1 in _O(m_) time, and building the _k_ Link-Cut structures _LC_<sub>1</sub>_,LC_<sub>2</sub>_,...,LC<sub>k</sub>_. The latter requires _O(kn_) MakeTree and link operations, each costing _O_(log_n_) amortized time, for a total initialization cost of \(O(m+k\cdot n\mathrm{log}n)\).

For each edge addition, HandleAddition calls TryAdd on at most _k_ forests. Each TryAdd call performs _O_(1) Link-Cut tree operations (FindRoot, cut, link), so the amortized cost per edge addition is _O(k_log_n_).

## 5 Restoration after Edge Removal

### 5.1 Edge-connectivity restoration algorithm

This section addresses restoring _k_-edge-connectivity after an edge deletion. Let _e_={_u,v_} be the deleted edge and let \(G'=G\backslash\{e\}\). If \(\lambda(G')\ge k\), no action is needed. Otherwise, the algorithm must compute a set of augmenting edges _E<sub>aug</sub>_ such that \(\lambda(G'\cup E_{aug})\ge k\). We compute a maximum _u-v_ flow in \(G'\) using Dinic’s algorithm \[4\], whose complexity on unit- capacity networks is \(O(\mathrm{min}(n^{2/3},m^{1/2})\cdot m)\) by Even and Tarjan \[5\], and use the resulting residual graph to identify _E<sub>aug</sub>_.

We model each undirected edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\) as a pair of directed arcs (_u,v_) and (_v,u_), each with unit capacity; for background on flow networks and residual graphs we refer to \[1\]. In the resulting residual graph _G<sub>f</sub>_, a saturated arc (_u,v_) with _f(u,v_)=1 is replaced by a backward arc (_v,u_) with residual capacity 2, while an unsaturated arc retains both directions with residual capacity 1.

The procedure HandleDeletion (Algorithm 4) works as follows. Given the deleted edge _e_={_u,v_}, it computes a maximum _u-v_ flow on \(G'=G\backslash\{e\}\). If the flow value is still at least _k_, the edge was redundant and no action is needed. Otherwise, let _G<sub>f</sub>_ denote the residual graph. The algorithm computes _S_, the set of vertices reachable from _u_ in _G<sub>f</sub>_, and _T_, the set of vertices from which _v_ is reachable in _G<sub>f</sub>_; both sets are obtained by BFS or DFS algorithm on _G<sub>f</sub>_.

The algorithm distinguishes two cases. If \(|S|\ge 2\) or \(|T|\ge 2\), there exists a pair \(u'\in S\), \(v'\in T\) with \(\{u',v'\}\neq\{u,v\}\); the algorithm adds \(\{u',v'\}\) to \(G'\) (Algorithm 4, lines 15-17). If _S_={_u_} and _T_={_v_}, the only edge from _S_ to _T_ is the deleted edge {_u,v_}, so instead the algorithm selects an arbitrary vertex \(w\in V\backslash\{u,v\}\) and adds the two edges {_u,w_} and {_w,v_} (Algorithm 4, lines 12-13).

### 5.2 Correctness and complexity of edge-connectivity restoration algorithm

We show that edges added by HandleDeletion increases the maximum _u-v_ flow by one (Lemma 6), and that the full procedure restores \(\lambda(G')\ge k\) (Theorem 7).

**Lemma 6.** _Let f be a maximum u-v flow in_ \(G'=G\backslash\{e\}\) _(e_={_u,v}), let G<sub>f</sub> be the residual graph, and define_ \(S=\{w\in V:w\text{\textit{is reachable from}}u\text{\textit{in}}G_f\}\) _and_ \(T=\{w\in V:v\text{\textit{is reachable from}}w\text{\textit{in}}G_f\}\)_. Then:_

1. \(S\cap T=\emptyset\).<tbc>

**Algorithm 4** Procedure for handling edge deletion operations. procedure HandleDeletion(e)
\((u,v)\leftarrow\) endpoints(e)
\(G\leftarrow G\backslash\{e\}\)
\(flow\leftarrow\) DinicMaxFlow(G,u,v)
if \(flow\ge k\) then
return
else if flow=k-1 then
\(G_f\leftarrow\) Residual Graph from Dinic’s execution on G
\(S\leftarrow\{w\in V|w\text{is reachable from}u\text{in}G_f\}\)
\(T\leftarrow\{w\in V|v\text{is reachable from}w\text{in}G_f\}\)
if \(S=\{u\}\wedge T=\{v\}\) then
\(u'\leftarrow\) arbitrarily chosen vertex in G
\(G\leftarrow G\cup\{\{u,u'\},\{u',v\}\}\)
else
\(u'\leftarrow\) arbitrarily chosen vertex from S
\(v'\leftarrow\) arbitrarily chosen vertex from T
\(G\leftarrow G\cup\{u',v'\}\)
end if
end if
end procedure V3 V1 V2 V4 V3 S V1 V2 T V4 V3 V1 V2 V4 V2 V3 V1 V4 V6 V5 T = {v2} V2 V3 V2 V3 S = {v1} V1 V4 V6 V5 V2 V3 V1 V4 V6 V5 (a) \(G'=G\backslash\{v_1,v_2\}\) (b) Residual graph _Gf_ (c) Augmented graph \(G''\) Figure 2: HandleDeletion({_v_1_,v_2}): single augmenting edge (\(|T|\ge 2\)). (a) \(G'=G\backslash\{v_1,v_2\}\) (b) Residual graph _Gf_ (c) Augmented graph \(G''\) Figure 3: HandleDeletion({_v_1_,v_2}): two augmenting edges (|_S_|=|_T_|=1).

_2. For any_ \(u'\in S\) _and_ \(v'\in T\)_, adding the undirected edge_ \(\{u',v'\}\) _to_ \(G'\) _increases the maximum u-v flow by one._

_Proof._<tbc>

1. If \(w\in S\cap T\), then _G<sub>f</sub>_ contains a path from _u_ to _w_ (since \(w\in S\)) and a path from _w_ to _v_ (since \(w\in T\)). Concatenating these paths yields an augmenting _u-v_ path, contradicting maximality of _f_.<tbc>

2. Adding edge \(\{u',v'\}\) to \(G'\) introduces the arc \((u',v')\) in the residual graph. Since \(u'\in S\), there is a path from _u_ to \(u'\) in _G<sub>f</sub>_; since \(v'\in T\), there is a path from \(v'\) to _v_ in _G<sub>f</sub>_. Concatenating these with the new arc gives an augmenting path from _u_ to _v_, increasing the flow by one.

**Theorem 7.** _Let_ \(G'=G\backslash\{e\}\) _where e_={_u,v_} _and_ \(\lambda(G')<k\)_. Let_ \(G''\) _be the augmented graph produced by Algorithm 4. Then_ \(\lambda(G'')\ge k\)_, and_ \(|E(G'')\backslash E(G')|\le 2\).

_Proof._ By Lemma 1, \(\lambda(u,v;G')=k-1\), and every cut of size less than _k_ in \(G'\) separates _u_ and _v_. The max _u-v_ flow in \(G'\) therefore equals _k_-1.

1. Case 1: \(|S|\ge 2\) or \(|T|\ge 2\). There exist \(u'\in S\) and \(v'\in T\) with \(\{u',v'\}\neq\{u,v\}\). The algorithm adds \(\{u',v'\}\). By Lemma 6, this increases the maximum _u-v_ flow to _k_. Since every cut of size less than _k_ separates _u_ and _v_ (Lemma 1), and the minimum _u-v_ cut now has size _k_, we have \(\lambda(G'')\ge k\). One edge is added.<tbc>

2. Case 2: _S_={_u_} and _T_={_v_}. The algorithm selects \(w\in V\backslash\{u,v\}\) and adds {_u,w_} and {_w,v_}. This creates the augmenting path \(u\rightarrow w\rightarrow v\), increasing the maximum _u-v_ flow to _k_. The same argument as Case 1 gives \(\lambda(G'')\ge k\). Two edges are added.

In both cases \(|E(G'')\backslash E(G')|\le 2\) holds.

The cost of Algorithm 4 is dominated by one execution of Dinic’s algorithm on the sparsified graph \(G'\). After applying the Nagamochi–Ibaraki sparsification \[12\], the graph has _m=O(kn_) edges while preserving all cuts of size at most _k_. By the Even–Tarjan bound \[5\], Dinic’s algorithm on a unit-capacity network runs in \(O(min(n^{2/3},m^{1/2})\cdot m)\) time. Substituting _m=O(kn_), this yields \(O(n^{2/3}\cdot kn)=O(kn^{5/3})\) and \(O((kn)^{1/2}\cdot kn)=O(k^{3/2}\cdot n^{3/2})\), respectively. Since _k_ is a fixed constant, \(k^{1/2}\cdot n^{1/2}<n^{2/3}\) for sufficiently large _n_, so the second branch dominates and the total cost is \(O(k^{3/2}\cdot n^{3/2})\). The subsequent BFS/DFS algorithm to compute _S_ and _T_ runs in _O(kn_) time and does not affect the asymptotic bound.
